body_markdown:
Our car hobby is entering a period of unprecedented transition. Baby boomers aren’t the only people who love old cars, but they’re the most numerous and the wealthiest, and their tastes have served as the primary force in the collector-car market for decades. In the coming years, they will be giving the keys over to younger enthusiasts. Hagerty estimates 12 million cars worth some $570 billion will change hands. The implications are massive.


This handoff is part of the Great Wealth Transfer, the term coined for what’s estimated to be a $124 *trillion* shift in assets between now and 2048. It is already happening and is shaping many aspects of the economy, from housing, where Baby Boomers are in some cases subsidizing home purchases for their adult children (while still building homes for themselves at an unprecedented rate), to so-called “skip-generation” vacations, where grandparents pay to take their grandkids on trips without their grown children.


Each car that changes hands will have a story. Hagerty recently collaborated with *Bloomberg’s* Hannah Elliott on the financial and intensely emotional personal aspects of this phenomenon in her piece, *[The Great Wealth Transfer Includes $570 Billion in Classic Cars](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-05-15/inheriting-a-classic-car-what-pitfalls-to-consider-tensions-to-avoid)* (paywall). We have ourselves looked at how to[prepare your own cars—and your kids—for the transition of automotive treasure](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/you-cant-take-em-with-you/) .


Zoom out, though, and there’s another concern worth considering: Will such a large-scale transition destabilize the classic car market? Here, we wanted to look deeper into what our data tell us about what we can expect for our hobby in the coming years.


## Older Enthusiasts Own Most of the Collector Cars


James Lipman


Let’s start with the one fact that is driving this whole discussion: older enthusiasts own *a lot* of collector cars. Most of them, in fact. Those who are 60 or older account for 63 percent of Hagerty-insured vehicles. This should come as no surprise. Baby Boomers, the largest and wealthiest cohort in American history, still dominate the economy and, per a recent report released by Visa, are sitting on $93 *trillion* in assets—more than Gen-Xers and Millennials combined. We also know that Baby Boomers have a special relationship with cars, particularly those of their 1960s youth, and fueled the exponential growth of the collector car market starting in the early 2000s.


It’s worth noting that many of these collectors have no immediate plans to sell and, in fact, remain extremely active buyers. Yet like death and taxes, it’s a certainty that someone else will eventually own these cars. In some cases, a Baby Boomer-owned car may wind up with a Gen–Z grandchild. Some collectors might sell their cars as they age; others may wind up in estate sales. Many, if not most, will ultimately hit the open market in one way or another.


## Millions of cars, billions of dollars


Our Automotive Intelligence team studied our insurance data to understand better how collectors’ buying-and-selling behavior shifts as they age. They also looked at broader data on aging and dying from the Social Security Administration (because if you’re dead, you’re probably selling rather than buying). They zeroed in on the ages 79 to 94. At the moment, only the very oldest of the Baby Boomers (those born in 1946 and 1947) are in this age group. Over the next 15 years, the vast majority of them will enter these golden years. During this span, our team projects this group will sell 12 million cars.


Michael Alan Ross


For context, Hagerty estimates the entire market consists of about 43 million vehicles. Looking back on the last 15 years, from 2010 to 2025, our Automotive Intelligence folks estimate that 5.1 million cars, from buyers and sellers of all ages, changed hands in the whole market. The Great Car Transfer thus represents *more than double* the collector vehicles sold in the last 15 years and a quarter ** of the market as a whole. Beyond the sheer volume of vehicles, there’s the value they represent: approximately $570 billion in today’s dollars.


[David Zenlea](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/david-zenlea/)


[David Zenlea](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/david-zenlea/)


## Who will buy all those cars?


Part of the angst about the Great Car Transfer comes from the size of the Baby Boomer generation, but it also derives from assumptions about young people and cars—namely that they don’t like ’em. Those assumptions are simply untrue. Millennial and Gen–Z car enthusiasts, along with Gen–Xers, have been entering the market for years now, and they’ve already had a profound influence on car collecting. Their ranks will continue to swell. Our main way of measuring who is entering the hobby is by looking at who is calling Hagerty (or visiting our website) for price quotes on insurance. In recent years, the majority of those quotes have been for the 60-and-younger crowd.


It’s worth noting here that many buyers likely won’t be young collectors, per se, but rather the “young old.” Think fifty-something empty nesters—the folks who are in their prime earning years and have disposable income. We thus don’t expect younger cohorts to suddenly and dramatically increase market share, despite the coming tsunami of cars headed to market. We may, however, observe an incremental change over the next 15 years as more and more older cars become available.


Cameron Neveu


We expect said influx to continue as they themselves grow older and accumulate more wealth (some of it inherited from those Baby Boomer parents). What’s more, we generally see that these younger collectors are interested in lots of the cars Baby Boomers currently own. Looking at the top ten most popular cars for each age group (see chart below), the plurality of cars are virtually the same.


Zooming out, our data show that, as you’d expect, older collectors tend to favor the oldest cars whereas younger collectors like newer cars, but that the differences aren’t quite as stark as is often discussed.


Our Automotive Intelligence team has put all this together into a forecast of younger generations’ capacity for pre-1974 vehicles, which make up the bulk of the cars in The Great Transfer. Based on Hagerty’s quote and policy data from younger generations, along with general demographic data, our team predicts that projected millennial buying power and interest in pre-’74 vehicles will outstrip the projected value of pre-’74 cars re-entering the market. Add in Gen X’s existing and Gen Z’s growing capacity, and we’re confident that the market will be able to absorb these older vehicles.


## A Question of Stability vs. Volatility


James Lipman


All this is not to say that we expect a seamless transition. For one thing, although younger people are generally interested in older cars, they’re not necessarily interested in *every* car their parents and grandparents liked—and they may not necessarily assign them the same value. There will be a divergence between those that are universally sought-after and the rest of the pack. The cars with shared generational interest shown above, and the pantheon of ’60s halo cars—your LS6 Chevelles and Hemi Cudas and the like—are the ones most likely to maintain their values. Vehicles more on the fringes of popularity, or those with less desirable options, may see their values begin to tread water.


It’s also worth noting that the older cars young collectors are interested in won’t necessarily appreciate. Older generations have already established their values. This is in contrast to newer cars, like the Mazda Miata, which, thanks to interest from younger collectors, are just beginning their transition from “used car” to “classic car.” In other words, the modern classics will likely appreciate more, whereas the older classics will simply remain stable.


Cameron Neveu


DW Burnett


Our Price Guide shows this is already happening. Whereas values for “hot” parts of the market—modern Ferraris, Japanese classics—zip up and down, more established segments like British and 1950s American cars have by and large leveled out. We expect that with the Great Car Transfer, more segments will begin to behave like the ’50s American and British cohorts.


To be clear, that’s not a bad thing. As much as classic car market watchers love to fixate on high-water-mark sales and double-digit appreciation, the essential goal of most real-world collectors is to be able to enjoy a vehicle for a few years and then sell it for around what they paid.


## Takeaway


Millions of times in the next 15 years, an old title will find a new drawer, and those keys will rest in a newer pocket. For some folks, it’ll be a treasure conferred; for others, a burden to process. There’s only so much we can predict about how all that change will play out. Based on what we see in the data, though, we are confident the cars Baby Boomers have loved, collected, and enjoyed will continue to be treasured by the generations to come.


Andrew Trahan
